synopsis: Simulation shortens validation, but cannot certify perception alone: the cited on-road evidence documents gaps across sensor types, including radar at CVPR 2024, lidar studies from 2023–2025, and camera studies from 2023 and December 2025 [f326, f471, f327, f328, f329]. Transferring road-based braking validation to quarry terrain and articulated machines is a larger change than transferring passenger-car tests to heavy trucks; no standards-body or industry-group study of that transfer was found, and sim-to-field transfer of machine motion and tuned thresholds remains unproven [f1236, f1248, f6421, f6558]. Sensor and environment fidelity is judged the hardest uncertainty, with dust the biggest off-road gap; idealized sensors can look realistic at tracking level while having the highest raw-data gap, and lidar mismatch increases at high rain rates [f10424, f11949, f4480, f4610]. Recorded-scene reconstruction is also constrained: on-road neural re-simulation degrades at viewpoint offsets of 1–4 m, while quantitative off-road validation of generative re-weathering was not found [f5213, f3825]. Construction and mining evidence from 2023–2026 supports synthetic data as augmentation rather than replacement for real data, including synthetic-only detection gaps and photometric divergence despite extensive domain randomization [f6686, f10580, f10581, f10584]. Planning should retain critical physical camera correlation and ongoing in-service feedback: the booklet calls monitoring the only route to close dust and glare model gaps over time, and warns that good virtual metrics can conceal field failures clustered by rain, dust, night or glare [f1737, f8053, f12455].
